items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the mental hygiene law, in relation to directing the commissioner of developmental disabilities to establish a procedure through which persons with developmental disabilities may choose to remain in a nonintegrated setting
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S3893

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the mental hygiene law, in relation to
directing the commissioner of developmental disabilities to establish
a procedure through which persons with developmental disabilities may
choose to remain in a nonintegrated setting

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

The purpose of this bill is to preserve the right of individuals with
developmental disabilities to choose to remain in a nonintegrated
setting. The bill also directs the Commissioner of the Office for
People With Developmental Disabilities to modify the State's agreement
on the closure of nonintegrated settings with the Centers for Medicare
and Medicaid Services, to allow for informed choice and to safeguard
the continued receipt of pertinent federal Medicaid funds.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1 establishes the act to be known as the "Employment First
Choice Act."

Section 2 states the legislative intent of the act, which is to
preserve an individual's right to choose whether to remain in a
nonintegrated setting.

Section 3 adds a new section 16.02 to article 16 of the mental hygiene
law, to direct the Commissioner of the Office for People With
Developmental Disabilities to establish a procedure for granting
accommodations to individuals who choose to remain in a nonintegrated
setting. This section also provides for the continued receipt of
services regardless of the choice of setting.

Section 4 directs the Commissioner of the Office for People With
Developmental Disabilities to resubmit its final New York plan to
increase competitive employment opportunities for people with
developmental disabilities, in order to continue eligibility for
federal funding for prevocational services.

Section 5 establishes the effective date.

JUSTIFICATION:

According to the New York State Office for People with Developmental
Disabilities' ("OPWDD") report to the legislature pursuant to chapter
60 of the laws of 2014 (the "Report"), New York State plans to fully
eliminate funding for nonintegrated settings, including sheltered
workshops, over the next six years. Therefore, all individuals now in
nonintegrated settings, irrespective of their wishes, will be required
to leave those facilities by 2020 or 2021. Many individuals with
developmental disabilities depend on these settings to socialize, to
earn a paycheck, and to improve and maintain their functional and
vocational skills.

Further, in its Report, OPWDD estimates that only half of the current
approximately 8,000 workshop participants will transition to an
integrated work setting when nonintegrated settings are discontinued.


The remaining participants will likely choose not to join an
integrated work setting because the setting is not appropriate for
their unique needs and does not fit into their individualized service
plan. The disruption and hardship that will be experienced by some
individuals who currently participate in a nonintegrated setting, but
who do not want to transition to any other activity, is alarming.
While these concerns were raised numerous times by public participants
in the twelve community dialogues held by OPWDD in 2014, this issue
was not addressed or resolved in the Report.

This result is contrary to the clear wording of the guiding U.S.
Supreme Court decision in Olmstead v. L.C., which held that states are
required to place individuals with developmental disabilities in
community settings rather than in institutions when, among other
conditions, "the transfer from institutional care to a less
restrictive setting is not opposed by the affected individual . . . ."

New York's rural areas, which extend through much of the State, pose
additional challenges that may further limit an individual's choice,
making the choice to remain in a nonintegrated setting even more
important to preserve. An absence of competitive employment
opportunities may prevent an individual from realizing the choice to
participate in an integrated setting. In addition, and also specific
to rural areas throughout the State, alternatives to employment are
limited, and some individuals may be transferred from a nonintegrated
setting to simply staying at home. As such, individuals who either
cannot obtain integrated employment and would prefer nonintegrated
employment to other alternatives, or who choose to remain in a
nonintegrated setting altogether, are at risk of being divested of
their most meaningful or engaging activity should a nonintegrated
environment be unavailable.

This bill, therefore, preserves the right of individuals with
developmental disabilities to choose to remain in a nonintegrated
setting. The bill also directs the Commissioner of OPWDD to modify the
State's agreement on the closure of nonintegrated settings with the
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, to allow for informed
choice and to safeguard the continued receipt of pertinent federal
Medicaid funds.

Finally, and critically, the bill echoes the intent of the U.S.
Supreme Court's decision in Olmstead v. L.C. as well as the provisions
of the Rhode Island Consent Decree. This landmark agreement between
the U.S. Department of Justice and the State of Rhode Island strongly
encourages integrated and competitive employment, but recognizes the
right of individuals with developmental disabilities who are current
sheltered workshop participants to remain in that setting if they
choose to do so.  Importantly, the bill also mirrors the Rhode Island
Consent Decree's process for making such an informed choice.

LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

This is a new bill.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

Undetermined.


EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect immediately.
